text:
Pythagoras - Wikipedia
Contents
Pythagoras
Pythagoras of Samos
[
a
]
(
Ancient Greek
:
Πυθαγόρας
;
c.
570
– c.
495
BC)
[
b
]
was an ancient
Ionian
Greek philosopher
,
polymath
, and the eponymous founder of
Pythagoreanism
.
His political and religious teachings were well known in
Magna Graecia
and influenced the philosophies of
Plato
,
Aristotle
, and, through them,
Western philosophy
. Modern scholars disagree regarding Pythagoras's education and influences, but most agree that he travelled to
Croton
in southern Italy around 530 BC, where he founded a school in which initiates were allegedly sworn to secrecy and lived a communal,
ascetic
lifestyle.
In antiquity, Pythagoras was credited with
mathematical
and scientific discoveries, such as the
Pythagorean theorem
,
Pythagorean tuning
, the
five regular solids
, the
theory of proportions
, the
sphericity of the Earth
, the identity of the
morning
and
evening stars
as the planet
Venus
, and the division of the globe into
five climatic zones
. He was reputedly the first man to call himself a philosopher ("lover of wisdom").
[
c
]
Historians debate whether Pythagoras made these discoveries and pronouncements, as some of the accomplishments credited to him likely originated earlier or were made by his colleagues or successors, such as
Hippasus
and
Philolaus
.
The teaching most securely identified with Pythagoras is the "transmigration of souls" or
metempsychosis
, which holds that every
soul
is
immortal
and, upon death,
enters into a new body
. He may have also devised the doctrine of
musica universalis
, which holds that the
planets
move according to
mathematical
ratios and thus resonate to produce an inaudible symphony of music. Following Croton's decisive victory over
Sybaris
in around 510 BC, Pythagoras's followers came into conflict with supporters of
democracy
, and their meeting houses were burned. Pythagoras may have been killed during this persecution, or he may have escaped to
Metapontum
and died there.
Pythagoras influenced Plato whose
dialogues
(especially
Timaeus
) exhibit Pythagorean ideas. A major revival of his teachings occurred in the first century BC among
Middle Platonists
, coinciding with the rise of
Neopythagoreanism
. Pythagoras continued to be regarded as a great philosopher throughout the
Middle Ages
and Pythagoreanism had an influence on scientists such as
Nicolaus Copernicus
,
Johannes Kepler
, and
Isaac Newton
. Pythagorean symbolism was also used throughout early modern
European esotericism
, and his teachings as portrayed in
Ovid
's
Metamorphoses
would later influence the modern vegetarian movement.
Life
No authentic writings of Pythagoras have survived,
[
4
]
[
5
]
and almost nothing is known for certain about his life.
[
6
]
[
7
]
The earliest sources on Pythagoras's life, from
Xenophanes
,
Heraclitus
,
Empedocles
,
Ion of Chios
, and
Herodotus
[
8
]
are brief, ambiguous, and often
satirical
.
[
9
]
[
10
]
The major sources on Pythagoras's life are three biographies from late antiquity written by
Diogenes Laërtius
,
Porphyry
, and
Iamblichus
, all of which are filled primarily with myths and legends
[
7
]
[
11
]
[
12
]
and which become longer and more fantastic in their descriptions of Pythagoras's achievements the more removed they are from Pythagoras's times.
[
11
]
[
12
]
However, Porphyry and Iamblichus also used some material taken from earlier writings in the 4th century BC by
Aristotle
's students
Dicaearchus
,
Aristoxenus
, and
Heraclides Ponticus
,
[
13
]
which, when it can be identified, is generally considered to be the most reliable.
[
13
]
There is not a single detail in the life of Pythagoras that stands uncontradicted. But it is possible, from a more or less critical selection of the data, to construct a plausible account.
—
Walter Burkert
, 1972
[
14
]
Herodotus
[
15
]
and
Isocrates
agree that Pythagoras was the son of Mnesarchus
[
16
]
[
17
]
and that he was born on the Greek island of
Samos
in the eastern
Aegean
.
[
4
]
[
17
]
[
18
]
Mnesarchus is said to have been a gem-engraver or a wealthy merchant,
[
19
]
[
20
]
[
21
]
but his ancestry is disputed and unclear.
[
d
]
Apollonius of Tyana
writes that Pythagoras's mother was Pythaïs, a woman who was said to be a descendant of
Ancaeus
, the mythical founder of Samos.
[
24
]
[
25
]
Iamblichus
tells the story that the Pythia prophesied to her while she was pregnant with him that she would give birth to a man supremely beautiful, wise, and beneficial to humankind, and Iamblichus also held to the belief that his mother descended from Ancaeus.
[
26
]
As to the date of his birth,
Aristoxenus
stated that Pythagoras left Samos in the reign of
Polycrates
, at the age of 40, which would give a date of birth around 570 BC.
[
27
]
Pythagoras's name led him to be associated with
Pythian
Apollo
(
Pūthíā
);
Aristippus of Cyrene
in the 4th century BC explained his name by saying, "He spoke [
ἀγορεύω
,
agoreúō
] the truth no less than did the Pythian [
πυθικός
,
puthikós
]".
[
26
]
During Pythagoras's formative years, Samos was a thriving cultural hub known for its feats of advanced architectural engineering, including the building of the
Tunnel of Eupalinos
, and for its riotous festival culture.
[
28
]
It was a major center of trade in the Aegean where traders brought goods from the
Near East
.
[
4
]
According to Christiane L. Joost-Gaugier, these traders almost certainly brought with them Near Eastern ideas and traditions.
[
4
]
Pythagoras's early life also coincided with the flowering of early Ionian
natural philosophy
.
[
17
]
[
29
]
He was a contemporary of the philosophers
Anaximander
and
Anaximenes
and of the historian
Hecataeus
, all of whom lived in
Miletus
, across the sea from Samos.
[
29
]
Modern scholarship has shown that the culture of
Archaic Greece
was heavily influenced by those of
Levantine
and
Mesopotamian
cultures, which appears to have been recognized by authors later in the Classical and Hellenistic periods, who attributed many of Pythagoras's unusual and unconventional beliefs to travels to far off lands, where he learned from those people himself.
[
30
]
The doctrine of
metempsychosis
, or reincarnation of the soul after death, which Herodotus and Diogenes Laertius had attributed to the Egyptians, led to an elaborate tale
[
31
]
where Pythagoras learned the
Egyptian language
from the
Pharaoh
Amasis II
himself, and then traveled to study with the Egyptian priests at
Diospolis
(Thebes), where he was the only foreigner ever to be granted the privilege of taking part in their worship.
[
30
]
Other ancient writers, however, claimed that Pythagoras had learned these teachings from the
Magi
in
Persia
or even from
Zoroaster
himself.
[
32
]
[
30
]
The
Phoenicians
are also reputed to have taught Pythagoras
arithmetic
and the
Chaldeans
to have taught him astronomy.
[
30
]
By the third century BC, Pythagoras was also reported to have studied under the
Jews
as well.
[
30
]
By the third century AD, Pythagoras was also reported by
Philostratus
to have studied under sages or
gymnosophists
in
India
and, according to
Iamblichus
, also with the
Celts
and
Iberians
.
[
30
]
Ancient sources also record Pythagoras having studied under a variety of native Greek thinkers.
[
33
]
Diogenes Laërtius asserts that Pythagoras later visited
Crete
, where he went to the
Cave of Ida
with
Epimenides
.
[
34
]
Some identify Hermodamas of Samos as a possible tutor.
[
33
]
[
35
]
Hermodamas represented the indigenous Samian
rhapsodic
tradition and his father Creophylos was said to have been the host of his rival poet
Homer
.
[
33
]
Others credit
Bias of Priene
, Thales,
[
36
]
or
Anaximander
(a pupil of Thales).
[
33
]
[
36
]
[
37
]
Other traditions claim the mythic bard
Orpheus
as Pythagoras's teacher, thus representing the
Orphic Mysteries
.
[
33
]
The Neoplatonists wrote of a "sacred discourse" Pythagoras had written on the gods in the
Doric Greek
dialect, which they believed had been dictated to Pythagoras by the Orphic priest Aglaophamus upon his initiation to the orphic Mysteries at
Leibethra
.
[
33
]
Iamblichus credited Orpheus with having been the model for Pythagoras's manner of speech, his spiritual attitude, and his manner of worship.
[
38
]
Iamblichus describes Pythagoreanism as a synthesis of everything Pythagoras had learned from Orpheus, from the Egyptian priests, from the
Eleusinian Mysteries
, and from other religious and philosophical traditions.
[
38
]
Contradicting all these reports, the novelist
Antonius Diogenes
, writing in the second century BC, reports that Pythagoras discovered all his doctrines himself by
interpreting dreams
.
[
33
]
Riedweg states that, although these stories are fanciful, Pythagoras's teachings were definitely influenced by Orphism to a noteworthy extent.
[
39
]
Of the various Greek sages claimed to have taught Pythagoras,
Pherecydes of Syros
is mentioned most often.
[
39
]
[
40
]
Similar miracle stories were told about both Pythagoras and Pherecydes, including one in which the hero predicts a shipwreck, one in which he predicts the conquest of
Messina
, and one in which he drinks from a well and predicts an earthquake.
[
39
]
Apollonius Paradoxographus
, a
paradoxographer
who may have lived in the second century BC, identified Pythagoras's
thaumaturgic
ideas as a result of Pherecydes's influence.
[
39
]
Another story, which may be traced to the Neopythagorean philosopher
Nicomachus
, tells that, when Pherecydes was old and dying on the island of
Delos
, Pythagoras returned to care for him and pay his respects.
[
39
]
Duris
, the historian and
tyrant
of Samos, is reported to have patriotically boasted of an epitaph supposedly penned by Pherecydes which declared that Pythagoras's wisdom exceeded his own.
[
39
]
On the grounds of all these references connecting Pythagoras with Pherecydes, Riedweg concludes that there may well be some historical foundation to the tradition that Pherecydes was Pythagoras's teacher.
[
39
]
Pythagoras and Pherecydes also appear to have shared similar views on the soul and the teaching of metempsychosis.
[
39
]
Porphyry repeats an account from
Antiphon
, who reported that, while he was still on Samos, Pythagoras founded a school known as the "semicircle".
[
41
]
[
42
]
Here, Samians debated matters of public concern.
[
41
]
[
42
]
Supposedly, the school became so renowned that the brightest minds in all of Greece came to Samos to hear Pythagoras teach.
[
41
]
Pythagoras himself dwelled in a secret cave, where he studied in private and occasionally held discourses with a few of his close friends.
[
41
]
[
42
]
Christoph Riedweg, a German scholar of early Pythagoreanism, states that it is entirely possible Pythagoras may have taught on Samos,
[
41
]
but cautions that Antiphon's account, which makes reference to a specific building that was still in use during his own time, appears to be motivated by Samian patriotic interest.
[
41
]
Around 530 BC, when Pythagoras was about forty years old, he left Samos.
[
4
]
[
17
]
[
43
]
[
44
]
His later admirers claimed that he left because he disagreed with the
tyranny
of
Polycrates
in Samos;
[
43
]
Riedweg notes that this explanation closely aligns with Nicomachus's emphasis on Pythagoras's purported love of freedom, but that Pythagoras's enemies portrayed him as having a proclivity towards tyranny.
[
43
]
Other accounts claim that Pythagoras left Samos because he was so overburdened with public duties in Samos, because of the high estimation in which he was held by his fellow-citizens.
[
45
]
He arrived in the Greek colony of Croton (today's
Crotone
, in
Calabria
) in what was then
Magna Graecia
.
[
17
]
[
44
]
[
46
]
[
47
]
[
48
]
All sources agree that Pythagoras was charismatic and quickly acquired great political influence in his new environment.
[
17
]
[
49
]
[
50
]
He served as an advisor to the elites in Croton and gave them frequent advice.
[
51
]
Later biographers tell fantastical stories of the effects of his eloquent speeches in leading the people of Croton to abandon their luxurious and corrupt way of life and devote themselves to the purer system which he came to introduce.
[
52
]
[
53
]
Suda
writes that Pythagoras had four children (Telauges, Mnesarchus, Myia and Arignote), and Diogenes Laertius records him as having had two brothers, Eunomus the elder and Tyrrhenus the second.
[
54
]
[
55
]
The wrestler
Milo of Croton
was said to have been a close associate of Pythagoras
[
56
]
and was credited with having saved the philosopher's life when a roof was about to collapse.
[
56
]
This association may have been the result of confusion with a different man named Pythagoras, who was an athletics trainer.
[
41
]
Pythagoras's emphasis on dedication and asceticism are credited with aiding in Croton's decisive victory over the neighboring colony of
Sybaris
in 510 BC.
[
57
]
After the victory, some prominent citizens of Croton proposed a
democratic constitution
, which the Pythagoreans rejected.
[
57
]
The supporters of democracy, headed by
Cylon
and Ninon, the former of whom is said to have been irritated by his exclusion from Pythagoras's brotherhood, roused the populace against them.
[
58
]
Followers of Cylon and Ninon attacked the Pythagoreans during one of their meetings, either in the house of Milo or in some other meeting-place.
[
59
]
[
60
]
Accounts of the attack are often contradictory and many probably confused it with the later anti-Pythagorean rebellions, such as the one in Metapontum in 454 BC.
[
58
]
[
61
]
The building was apparently set on fire,
[
59
]
and many of the assembled members perished;
[
59
]
only the younger and more active members managed to escape.
[
62
]
Sources disagree regarding whether Pythagoras was present when the attack occurred and, if he was, whether or not he managed to escape.
[
14
]
[
60
]
In some accounts, Pythagoras was not at the meeting when the Pythagoreans were attacked because he was on Delos tending to the dying Pherecydes.
[
60
]
According to another account from Dicaearchus, Pythagoras was at the meeting and managed to escape,
[
63
]
leading a small group of followers to the nearby city of
Locris
, where they pleaded for sanctuary, but were denied.
[
63
]
They reached the city of
Metapontum
, where they took shelter in the temple of the
Muses
and died there of starvation after forty days without food.
[
14
]
[
59
]
[
63
]
[
64
]
Another tale recorded by Porphyry claims that, as Pythagoras's enemies were burning the house, his devoted students laid down on the ground to make a path for him to escape by walking over their bodies across the flames like a bridge.
[
63
]
Pythagoras managed to escape, but was so despondent at the deaths of his beloved students that he committed suicide.
[
63
]
A different legend reported by both Diogenes Laërtius and Iamblichus states that Pythagoras almost managed to escape, but that he came to a fava bean field and refused to run through it, since doing so would violate his teachings, so he stopped instead and was killed.
[
63
]
This story seems to have originated from the writer Neanthes, who told it about later Pythagoreans, not about Pythagoras himself.
[
63
]
Teachings
Although the exact details of Pythagoras's teachings are uncertain,
[
65
]
[
66
]
it is possible to reconstruct a general outline of his main ideas.
[
65
]
[
67
]
Aristotle writes at length about the teachings of the Pythagoreans,
[
68
]
[
69
]
but without mentioning Pythagoras directly.
[
68
]
[
69
]
One of Pythagoras's main doctrines appears to have been
metempsychosis
,
[
70
]
[
71
]
[
72
]
[
73
]
[
74
]
the belief that all
souls
are immortal and that, after death, a soul is transferred into a new body.
[
70
]
[
73
]
This teaching is referenced by Xenophanes, Ion of Chios, and Herodotus.
[
70
]
[
75
]
The earliest source on Pythagoras's metempsychosis is a satirical poem probably written after his death by the Greek philosopher
Xenophanes of Colophon
(
c.
570
– c.
478
BC), who had been one of his contemporaries,
[
76
]
[
77
]
in which Xenophanes describes Pythagoras interceding on behalf of a
dog
that is being beaten, professing to recognize in its cries the voice of a departed friend.
[
e
]
[
10
]
[
76
]
[
68
]
Nothing whatsoever, however, is known about the nature or mechanism by which Pythagoras believed metempsychosis to occur.
[
78
]
Empedocles
alludes in one of his poems that Pythagoras may have claimed to possess the ability to recall his former incarnations.
[
79
]
Diogenes Laërtius reports an account from
Heraclides Ponticus
that Pythagoras told people that he had lived four previous lives that he could remember in detail.
[
80
]
[
81
]
[
82
]
The first of these lives was as
Aethalides
the son of
Hermes
, who granted him the ability to remember all his past incarnations.
[
83
]
Next, he was incarnated as
Euphorbus
, a minor hero from the
Trojan War
briefly mentioned in the
Iliad
.
[
84
]
He then became the philosopher
Hermotimus
,
[
85
]
who recognized the shield of Euphorbus in the temple of Apollo.
[
85
]
His final incarnation was as Pyrrhus, a fisherman from
Delos
.
[
85
]
One of his past lives, as reported by
Dicaearchus
, was as a beautiful courtesan.
[
71
]
[
86
]
Another belief attributed to Pythagoras was that of the "
harmony of the spheres
",
[
90
]
[
91
]
which maintained that the planets and stars move according to mathematical equations, which correspond to musical notes and thus produce an inaudible symphony.
[
90
]
[
91
]
According to Porphyry, Pythagoras taught that the seven
Muses
were actually the
seven planets
singing together.
[
92
]
The so-called Pythagoreans applied themselves to mathematics, and were the first to develop this science; and through studying it they came to believe that its principles are the principles of everything.
—
Aristot. Met. 1
, 985b
Modern scholars typically ascribe these discoveries to the later Pythagorean philosopher
Philolaus of Croton
(
c.
470
– c.
385
BC), whose extant fragments are the earliest texts to describe the numerological and musical theories that were later ascribed to Pythagoras.
[
93
]
In his landmark study
Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism
, Walter Burkert argues that Pythagoras was a charismatic political and religious teacher,
[
94
]
but that the number philosophy attributed to him was really an innovation by Philolaus.
[
95
]
According to Burkert, Pythagoras never dealt with numbers at all, let alone made any noteworthy contribution to mathematics.
[
94
]
Burkert argues that the only mathematics the Pythagoreans ever actually engaged in was simple,
proofless
arithmetic
,
[
96
]
but that these arithmetic discoveries did contribute significantly to the beginnings of mathematics.
[
97
]
For the later Pythagoreans, Pythagoras was credited with devising the
tetractys
, the triangular figure of four rows which add up to the "perfect" number, ten.
[
87
]
[
98
]
The Pythagoreans regarded the tetractys as a symbol of utmost mystical importance.
[
88
]
Iamblichus, in his
Life of Pythagoras
, states that the tetractys was "so admirable, and so divinised by those who understood [it]," that Pythagoras's students would swear oaths by it.
[
88
]
[
99
]
This shouldn't be confused with a simplified version known today as "
Pythagorean numerology
", involving a variant of an isopsephic technique known – among other names – as
pythmenes
'
roots
'
[
100
]
or
'
base numbers
'
,
[
101
]
by means of which the base values of letters in a word were mathematically reduced by addition or division, in order to obtain a single value from one to nine for the whole name or word.
[
100
]
Pythagoreanism
Both
Plato
and
Isocrates
state that, above all else, Pythagoras was known as the founder of a new way of life.
[
102
]
[
103
]
[
104
]
The organization Pythagoras founded at Croton was called a "school",
[
105
]
[
106
]
but, in many ways, resembled a
monastery
.
[
107
]
The adherents were bound by a
vow
to Pythagoras and each other, for the purpose of pursuing the
religious
and
ascetic
observances, and of studying his religious and
philosophical
theories.
[
108
]
The members of the sect
shared all their possessions in common
[
109
]
and were devoted to each other to the exclusion of outsiders.
[
110
]
[
111
]
Ancient sources record that the Pythagoreans ate meals in common after the manner of the
Spartans
.
[
112
]
[
113
]
One Pythagorean
maxim
was "
koinà tà phílōn
" ("All things in common among friends").
[
109
]
Both Iamblichus and Porphyry provide detailed accounts of the organization of the school, although the primary interest of both writers is not historical accuracy, but rather to present Pythagoras as a divine figure, sent by the
gods
to benefit mankind.
[
114
]
Iamblichus, in particular, presents the "Pythagorean Way of Life" as a pagan alternative to the Christian monastic communities of his own time.
[
107
]
For Pythagoreans, the highest reward humans could attain was for their soul to join in the life of the gods and thus escape the cycle of reincarnation.
[
115
]
Two groups existed within early Pythagoreanism: the
mathematikoi
("learners") and the
akousmatikoi
("listeners").
[
116
]
[
117
]
The
akousmatikoi
are traditionally identified by scholars as "old believers" in mysticism, numerology, and religious teachings;
[
117
]
whereas the
mathematikoi
are traditionally identified as a more intellectual, modernist faction who were more rationalist and scientific.
[
117
]
Gregory cautions that there was probably not a sharp distinction between them and that many Pythagoreans probably believed the two approaches were compatible.
[
117
]
The study of mathematics and music may have been connected to the worship of Apollo.
[
118
]
The Pythagoreans believed that music was a purification for the soul, just as medicine was a purification for the body.
[
92
]
One anecdote of Pythagoras reports that when he encountered some drunken youths trying to break into the home of a virtuous woman, he sang a solemn tune with long
spondees
and the boys' "raging willfulness" was quelled.
[
92
]
The Pythagoreans also placed particular emphasis on the importance of
physical exercise
;
[
107
]
therapeutic
dancing
, daily morning walks along
scenic routes
, and
athletics
were major components of the Pythagorean lifestyle.
[
107
]
Moments of contemplation at the beginning and end of each day were also advised.
[
119
]
Pythagorean teachings were known as "symbols" (
symbola
)
[
120
]
and members took a vow of silence that they would not reveal these symbols to non-members.
[
120
]
[
103
]
[
121
]
Those who did not obey the laws of the community were expelled
[
122
]
and the remaining members would erect
tombstones
for them as though they had died.
[
122
]
A number of "oral sayings" (
akoúsmata
) attributed to Pythagoras have survived,
[
68
]
[
123
]
dealing with how members of the Pythagorean community should perform sacrifices, how they should honor the gods, how they should "move from here", and how they should be buried.
[
124
]
Many of these sayings emphasize the importance of ritual purity and avoiding defilement.
[
125
]
[
74
]
Other extant oral sayings forbid Pythagoreans from breaking bread, poking fires with swords, or picking up crumbs
